In March, while still in his senior year, he co-authored the paper "Attention Residuals," which was shared by Elon Musk and later applied to Kimi K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter model. He had joined Kimi at 16 after being hired by Du Yulun, and recently announced his departure, saying "there is more worth exploring." Around the same time, Silicon Valley investor Deedy Das described an unnamed 17-year-old with five job offers from top SF AI labs, each worth over $1 million—widely believed to be Chen.

Chen grew up in Shenzhen and was largely self-taught in AI, using models to study papers and GitHub projects rather than traditional courses. A technical blog on DeltaNet led to a seven-week internship at Tilde Research in Palo Alto at 16. He was advised to act like a CEO, not an intern, which shaped his approach to operations, fundraising, and strategy.

His story reflects a broader AI talent war. Companies now recruit before graduation, with PhD graduates in large-model directions reportedly earning over 6 million yuan, and top young researchers receiving offers like Meta's roughly $250 million package for Matt Deitke. Internships at Tencent and ByteDance now offer open-ended pay and project leadership.
